Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2013 Jul 18. Published in final edited form as: Psychol Assess. 2011 May 2;23(4):834–847. doi: 10.1037/a0023621 Abstract The purpose of this study was to evaluate the psychometric properties of an audio computer-assisted self-interviewing Web-based software application called the Social Information Processing Application (SIP-AP) that was designed to assess social information processing skills in boys in 3rd through 5th grades. This study included a racially and ethnically diverse sample of 244 boys ages 8 through 12 (M = 9.4) from public elementary schools in 3 states. The SIP-AP includes 8 videotaped vignettes, filmed from the first-person perspective, that depict common misunderstandings among boys. Each vignette shows a negative outcome for the victim and ambiguous intent on the part of the perpetrator. Boys responded to 16 Web-based questions representing the 5 social information processing mechanisms, after viewing each vignette. Parents and teachers completed measures assessing boys’ antisocial behavior. Confirmatory factor analyses revealed that a model positing the original 5 cognitive mechanisms fit the data well when the items representing prosocial cognitions were included on their own factor, creating a 6th factor. The internal consistencies for each of the 16 individual cognitions as well as for the 6 cognitive mechanism scales were excellent. Boys with elevated scores on 5 of the 6 cognitive mechanisms exhibited more antisocial behavior than boys whose scores were not elevated. These findings highlight the need for further research on the measurement of prosocial cognitions or cognitive strengths in boys in addition to assessing cognitive deficits. Findings suggest that the SIP-AP is a reliable and valid tool for use in future research of social information processing skills in boys. Keywords: social information processing, antisocial behavior, aggression, Web-based assessment, social cognitive deficits ---------------------------------------- Social information processing (SIP) patterns in youth refer to a series of cognitive mechanisms associated with making decisions about interpersonal behavior. A conceptual framework was proposed within the developmental literature that provides a coherent structure and flow to understanding the processes associated with social decision making (Crick & Dodge, 1994) that has had a tremendous impact on research across a wide range of fields in psychology. For example, the SIP theory has stimulated efforts to examine the etiology and growing complexity of social cognitive patterns across development (Fontaine, Yang, Dodge, Bates, & Pettit, 2008). In addition, this model has provided a rich foundation for research in the field of developmental psychopathology, such that biases or extremes in SIP responses have been found among aggressive and delinquent youths (Dodge, Coie, & Lynam, 2006). From a prevention science perspective, the SIP model has been translated into strategies for teaching social cognitive skills and reorienting cognitive biases to contribute to the prevention of aggressive, delinquent, and substance abusing behaviors (e.g., Fast Track, Conduct Problems Prevention Research Group, 1992; Metropolitan Area Child Study Intervention, Eron et al., 2002; Making Choices, Fraser, Nash, Galinsky, & Darwin, 2000; Second Step, Grossman et al., 1997). Similarly, school-based social emotional learning programs aimed at teaching social skills and enhancing academic functioning have also successfully utilized the SIP model as a conceptual foundation for their curriculum objectives (Durlak, Weissberg, Dymnicki, Taylor, & Schellinger, 2011). Finally, in the clinical child and psychiatric literatures, cognitive-behavioral intervention programs for aggressive and delinquent youths have been successfully developed and evaluated in randomized controlled trials to treat SIP cognitive deficits to reduce antisocial behavior (e.g., Coping Power, Lochman & Wells, 2002a, 2002b, 2004, 2005). Despite this well-developed body of research on SIP, there remains a need for a psychometrically strong measure of the cognitive mechanisms composing the SIP model that can be used for a wide range of purposes, and this forms the main goal of the current study. The SIP Model and Aggression The reformulated SIP model includes five cognitive mechanisms: (a) encoding of internal and external cues, (b) interpretation of these cues, (c) goal selection, (d) access to or construction of possible responses, and (e) response decision (Crick & Dodge, 1994). Each of the five SIP mechanisms has been related to aggressive behavior in correlation studies. In fact, SIP mechanisms are incrementally predictive of aggressive behavior over time (Dodge & Price, 1994), and longitudinal studies have reported that patterns of deviant SIP processing may be causally related to aggressive responding across development (Zelli, Dodge, Lochman, Laird, & Conduct Problems Prevention Research Group, 1999). In addition, Guerra and Slaby (1990) reported that changes in social cognitive mediators, including SIP skills, after exposure to a cognitive mediation training program, were associated with reductions in aggressive behavior. Similarly, Lochman and Wells (2002a) reported that changes in several SIP cognitions partially mediated the impact of a social cognitive intervention program on school behavior problems, delinquency, and substance use. Aggressive behavior is stable during childhood and adolescence and is more stable over time than many other behaviors (Lochman, Whidby, & Fitzgerald, 2000). fetched_contents.text: Social information processing problems related to reactive and proactive aggression of adolescents in residential treatment Introduction Antisocial behaviours in adolescents have a major impact on society and brings considerable costs (Scott, S., et al., 2001, Cohen, M.A. and Piquero, A.R., 2009). Adolescents showing severe antisocial behaviours may end up in the juvenile justice system, although such an imposed intervention does not always lead to reduction of problematic behaviours; many show recidivism after two years (Wartna, B.S.J., et al., 2006, Wartna, B. S. J., et al., 2012). Since 2008, a new compulsory residential treatment programme was implemented in the Netherlands, specifically aimed at adolescents with severe problem behaviours. Research has shown that adolescents in this residential treatment programme predominantly showed externalizing problem behaviours (98%) (Van Dam, Nijhof, Scholte, & Veerman, 2010). Evaluation of treatment progress of adolescents in the residential programme has shown significant decreases in externalizing problem behaviours as reported by adolescents and parents. However, group care worker ratings showed a worsening of externalizing behaviours during admittance (Nijhof, Veerman, Engels, & Scholte, 2011). As such, rigorous interventions specifically aimed to reduce severe externalizing behaviours (and recidivism) in adolescents do not necessarily have the desired effect. This could be due to the generic nature of these interventions, which are possibly not sufficiently tailored to differences within externalizing behaviours of the adolescents. In order to provide more tailored interventions, it is important to gain more knowledge on the underlying processes of different types of externalizing behaviours. It has been suggested that the origin of aggressive and rule-breaking behaviours lies within one or more problems in social information processing (Crick & Dodge, 1994). As such, the current study will investigate different types of aggression and the underlying social information processing problems in a group of adolescents with severe externalizing behavioural problems in a residential treatment programme. The social information processing (SIP) model assumes that in a social situation, behaviour is achieved by six sequential steps, i.e. (1) encoding of external and internal cues, (2) interpretation of cues, including attributions, (3) goal clarification or selection, (4) response generation, and (5) response decision, including response evaluation, outcome expectancies, self-efficacy, response selection and the last step involving (6) behavioural enactment (Crick & Dodge; 1994). Problems in each one of these steps may lead to problematic behavioural responses, e.g. aggression. Ultimately, researching the underling SIP problems of aggression may inform a more tailored treatment for aggressive youth. The first two SIP steps (encoding and interpretation of cues) are thought to guide interpretation and understanding of the current social situation. It has been shown that aggressive children are less likely to use relevant social cues compared to non-aggressive children (Dodge & Tomlin, 1987). Hostile attribution bias or style (HAS) is the tendency to attribute hostile intent to others, which involves encoding and interpretation. A meta-analysis has confirmed that HAS is linked to aggression in several populations and across different ages (Orobio de Castro, Veerman, Koops, Bosch, & Monshouwer, 2002). Furthermore, research supports the hypothesis that hostile attribution contributes to aggressive behaviour over time, predicting future aggressive behaviour (Dodge, 2006). As such, the early steps of social information processing involving encoding and interpretation seem to play a significant role in aggressive behaviour through hostile attribution biases. The role of late steps in social information processing in aggressive behaviour has not been researched as extensively. The steps of (3) goal clarification or selection, (4) response generation have received little or no attention. It has been shown that pre-adolescent aggressive boys generate more aggressive responses and evaluate aggressive responses less negatively (Orobio de Castro, Merk, Koops, Veerman, & Bosch, 2005). Response decision (5) has been shown to have a mediating role in the relation between hostile attribution and antisocial behaviour, especially in adolescents with well-developed cognitive processing capacities (Fontaine, R.G., 2010, Fontaine, R.G., et al., 2010). It has been shown that youth who have problems in both early and late SIP steps, show higher externalizing problems then youth characterized by either early or late SIP problems (Lansford et al., 2006). The present study focuses on both early and late SIP steps, and investigates social information processing problems and its relation with different types of aggression. Aggressive behaviour can be divided into subtypes based on motive or function. In this respect, defensive aggression is labelled as reactive aggression, whereas an instrumental or offensive act is labelled as proactive aggression (Vitiello & Stoff, 1997). According to this division, reactive aggression emerges from the (subjective) experience that a given situation is hostile, and is a reaction to an aversive event or anticipated threat as part of a defence mechanism. Proactive aggression however, is driven by the anticipation of reward and is offensive or premeditated in nature (Merk, Orobio de Castro, Koops, & Matthys, 2005). These subtypes of aggression are thought to theoretically differ in function and underlying mechanisms, in which reactive aggression involves hostile attributions and is frustrations based, while proactive stems from positive outcome learning (Merk et al., 2005). Affiliation * 1 Vanderbilt University, Nashville, Tennessee 37203. * PMID: 3694454 * DOI: 10.1037//0022-3514.53.6.1146 Abstract We examined social-information-processing mechanisms (e.g., hostile attributional biases and intention-cue detection deficits) in chronic reactive and proactive aggressive behavior in children's peer groups. In Study 1, a teacher-rating instrument was developed to assess these behaviors in elementary school children (N = 259). Reactive and proactive scales were found to be internally consistent, and factor analyses partially supported convergent and discriminant validities. In Study 2, behavioral correlates of these forms of aggression were examined through assessments by peers (N = 339). Both types of aggression related to social rejection, but only proactively aggressive boys were also viewed as leaders and as having a sense of humor. In Study 3, we hypothesized that reactive aggression (but not proactive aggression) would occur as a function of hostile attributional biases and intention-cue detection deficits. Four groups of socially rejected boys (reactive aggressive, proactive aggressive, reactive-proactive aggressive, and nonaggressive) and a group of average boys were presented with a series of hypothetical videorecorded vignettes depicting provocations by peers and were asked to interpret the intentions of the provocateur (N = 117). Only the two reactive-aggressive groups displayed biases and deficits in interpretations. In Study 4, attributional biases and deficits were found to be positively correlated with the rate of reactive aggression (but not proactive aggression) displayed in free play with peers (N = 127). These studies supported the hypothesis that attributional biases and deficits are related to reactive aggression but not to proactive aggression. Empirical evidence for reactive aggression shows that the most consistently linked deficits are attributional biases and intention-cue detection deficits, especially hostile attribution bias. The classic 1987 study in *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* explicitly supports the hypothesis that attributional biases and deficits are related to reactive aggression but not to proactive aggression [N5-F3]. The same source reports that only reactive-aggressive groups displayed biases and deficits in interpretations when presented with hypothetical provocations [N5-F3]. This means that reactive aggression is associated with misinterpreting ambiguous social cues as hostile, rather than with deficits in later stages of processing.

Interpretation and evaluation are closely tied to anger and retaliation in reactive aggression. The N2 evidence states that reactive aggression is thought to involve difficulties in encoding and interpreting cues, and that hostile attribution bias is the tendency to attribute hostile intent to others [N2-F2]. It also notes that hostile attribution has been linked to aggression in several populations and across different ages, and that it predicts future aggressive behavior over time [N2-F2]. Additionally, the broader SIP framework in N2-F2 says that SIP problems may lead to problematic behavioral responses, such as aggression, and that aggressive children are less likely to use relevant social cues compared to non-aggressive children [N2-F2]. This implies that deficits in interpretation are not just about noticing cues, but about evaluating them in a hostile light, which then fuels anger and retaliatory behavior.

Evaluation matters because the SIP model includes response decision as part of the sequence, and the N2-F2 excerpt indicates that response decision has a mediating role in the relation between hostile attribution and antisocial behavior, especially in adolescents with well-developed cognitive processing capacities [N2-F2]. So reactive aggression is not only about how children interpret cues, but also about how they evaluate those interpretations and choose retaliatory responses.

Evidence on age and gender variation is limited in the provided material, but there is enough context to note important developmental nuances. The N4 evidence shows that emotion regulation deficits are linked to aggressive behavior and that SIP deficits are part of the broader developmental literature on aggression [N4-R4]. It also mentions that early peer aggression may represent an important pathway to pervasive social maladjustment [N4-R1]. The N2 evidence, however, focuses more on adolescents in residential treatment and on boys with aggressive behavior problems, suggesting that the most direct empirical reports are strongest in older children and adolescents [N2-F2]. The N4 excerpt also notes that boys were more aggressive than girls, but gender did not interact significantly with years of rejection [N4-R3]. This implies that boys may be more likely to show reactive aggression overall, but the provided evidence does not establish a strong gender moderation in SIP deficits per se.

Overall, the evidence for reactive aggression is strongest for deficits in encoding and interpretation, especially hostile attribution bias and intention-cue detection deficits [N5-F3][N2-F2]. These deficits correlate with anger and retaliation because they lead to hostile interpretations of ambiguous situations and then to aggressive responses [N2-F2]. The evidence suggests some age-specificity, with clearer support in adolescents and boys, but the provided material is thinner on precise developmental gradients [N4-R1][N4-R3].

The social information processing model relevant to aggression is best understood as a sequence of cognitive steps that determine how children interpret and respond to social situations. The N1-F1 excerpt provides the clearest framework: the SIP model includes five cognitive mechanisms—encoding of internal and external cues, interpretation of these cues, goal selection, access to or construction of possible responses, and response decision [N1-F1]. It also states that SIP patterns in youth refer to a series of cognitive mechanisms associated with making decisions about interpersonal behavior [N1-F1]. This is important because it maps the stages to aggression through the way children process social information, not just through emotional reactivity.

For interpreting social cues, the most relevant stages are encoding and interpretation. The N1-F1 excerpt says that aggressive behavior is associated with deficits in each of the SIP steps, and that SIP mechanisms are incrementally predictive of aggressive behavior over time [N1-F1]. The same source says that changes in SIP skills after cognitive mediation training were associated with reductions in aggressive behavior [N1-F1]. That makes encoding and interpretation especially important because they are the first steps in understanding the social environment. The N2-F2 excerpt reinforces this by saying that the first two SIP steps—encoding and interpretation of cues—are thought to guide interpretation and understanding of the current social situation [N2-F2]. It also notes that aggressive children are less likely to use relevant social cues compared to non-aggressive children [N2-F2].

Evaluation and interpretation differ between reactive and proactive aggression in the model. The N2-F2 excerpt says that reactive aggression involves difficulties in encoding and interpreting cues, and that proactive aggression involves different SIP problems [N2-F2]. The classic 1987 N5-F3 study supports the hypothesis that attributional biases and deficits are related to reactive aggression but not to proactive aggression [N5-F3]. That means reactive aggression is tied to deficits in how children interpret ambiguous social cues, especially hostile attribution bias, whereas proactive aggression is tied to other SIP deficits. The N1-F1 excerpt adds that response decision has a mediating role in the relation between hostile attribution and antisocial behavior [N1-F1], so evaluation is not separate from interpretation in the model—it is part of the broader processing sequence.

Deficits in each stage predict aggressive behavior in different ways. The N1-F1 evidence shows that SIP mechanisms are incrementally predictive of aggressive behavior over time and that deviant SIP processing may be causally related to aggressive responding [N1-F1]. The N2-F2 excerpt says that SIP problems may lead to problematic behavioral responses, such as aggression [N2-F2]. It also notes that aggressive children are less likely to use relevant social cues [N2-F2], which points to encoding deficits. The N5-F3 evidence supports the hypothesis that hostile attribution and intention-cue detection deficits are specifically linked to reactive aggression [N5-F3]. The broader SIP framework in N1-F1 suggests that deficits can occur across all steps, but the evidence provided is strongest for early-stage deficits in reactive aggression and for later-stage or response-related deficits in proactive aggression [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2].

In sum, the SIP model maps most clearly onto aggression through encoding and interpretation as the stages most relevant to interpreting social cues [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Evaluation is integrated into the later stages, especially response decision, and reactive aggression is best explained by deficits in hostile attribution and intention-cue detection [N5-F3][N2-F2]. Proactive aggression, by contrast, is associated with different SIP problems, including response generation and strategic processing, rather than the same interpretation deficits [N3-R2][N3-R5].

## How deficiencies in different stages of social information processing help distinguish reactive from proactive aggression in children

Social information processing (SIP) deficits are useful for distinguishing reactive from proactive aggression because they reflect different cognitive pathways: reactive aggression is best explained by early-stage interpretation deficits, especially hostile attribution bias and intention-cue detection, while proactive aggression is better explained by later-stage response generation and strategic processing deficits [N5-F3][N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-R5]. This distinction is not merely about severity or frequency; it is about function. Reactive aggression arises when children misinterpret ambiguous social cues as hostile, leading to anger and retaliation, whereas proactive aggression emerges from anticipation of reward and from deficits in generating or executing strategic, premeditated responses [N2-F2][N3-R5][N6-R3].

### 1) Specific deficits that better predict one aggression style than the other

The evidence is strongest for **reactive aggression**. The classic 1987 study shows that attributional biases and deficits are specifically related to reactive aggression but not to proactive aggression [N5-F3]. That same source reports that only reactive-aggressive groups displayed biases and deficits in interpretations when presented with hypothetical provocations [N5-F3]. The SIP model framework in the provided material also links hostile attribution bias and poor cue use to aggression, with aggressive children being less likely to use relevant social cues [N2-F2].

For **proactive aggression**, the evidence is less direct but still meaningful. The SIP literature indicates that proactive aggression involves different SIP problems than reactive aggression, and that it is associated with response generation and strategic processing deficits rather than hostile attribution deficits [N3-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence also points to deficits in response generation and strategic planning as being central to proactive aggression, while early-stage interpretation deficits are not the main predictors [N3-R2][N3-R5]. In other words, proactive aggression is better predicted by later-stage deficits in generating and executing strategic responses than by the same interpretation deficits that drive reactive aggression [N3-R2][N3-R5].

### 2) How deficits interact across stages rather than in isolation

The SIP model itself is presented as a sequence of steps: encoding, interpretation, goal selection, response generation, and response decision [N1-F1]. The provided evidence repeatedly emphasizes that these stages are not isolated; they interact. The N1-F1 excerpt states that SIP mechanisms are incrementally predictive of aggressive behavior over time, and that deviant SIP processing may be causally related to aggressive responding across development [N1-F1]. The N2-F2 excerpt expands on this by noting that SIP problems may occur across encoding, interpretation, goal clarification, response generation, and response decision [N2-F2].

This sequential structure matters because deficits can cascade across stages. For example, a child may misinterpret a cue (encoding/interpretation), then retrieve an aggressive response (response access), then select and execute it (response decision), with emotion regulation and schema activation shaping each step [N2-F2][N6-R5]. The N6-R5 excerpt adds that aggressive response access predicted aggression and may mediate between schemas and behavior [N6-R5]. This means that SIP deficits do not act in isolation; they are embedded in a broader network of cognitive and regulatory processes.

The evidence also suggests that environmental provocation can amplify these deficits. The N6-R4 excerpt indicates that peer social rejection can lead children to respond with increased reactive and proactive aggression [N6-R4]. This shows that SIP deficits interact with external contexts, making aggression more likely when provocation is present.

### 3) Mechanisms linking SIP deficits to aggression

The evidence points to several mechanisms through which SIP deficits contribute to aggression:

- **Attributional biases and encoding errors** directly contribute to aggression by distorting the initial processing of social information. Hostile attribution bias and intention-cue detection deficits are especially linked to reactive aggression [N5-F3][N2-F2]. These deficits create hostile interpretations of ambiguous situations, which then fuel anger and retaliation [N2-F2].
- **Schemas, response access, and emotion regulation** are key mediators. The N6-R5 excerpt states that aggressive response access predicted aggression and may mediate between schemas and behavior [N6-R5]. The N6-R3 excerpt suggests that intervening with proactively aggressive children who exhibit response-generation deficits should include developing prosocial versus instrumental responses [N6-R3]. The N4-R4 excerpt notes that emotion regulation deficits are directly linked to aggressive behavior and that SIP deficits are part of the broader developmental literature on aggression [N4-R4].

Taken together, these mechanisms show that SIP deficits contribute to aggression through a chain of biased encoding, hostile interpretation, schema activation, response retrieval, and emotion-regulated execution [N5-F3][N2-F2][N6-R5][N4-R4].

### 4) Limitations and gaps in the evidence

The evidence supports the distinction between reactive and proactive aggression, but it is uneven. The support for reactive aggression is much stronger, particularly around hostile attribution and intention-cue detection [N5-F3][N2-F2]. Proactive aggression is supported mainly through theoretical distinction and some indirect evidence on response generation and strategic processing [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This means the evidence is more robust for reactive aggression than for proactive aggression.

Another limitation is that the developmental picture is not fully resolved. The evidence suggests some age-specificity, with clearer support in adolescents and boys, but it does not establish a robust age trajectory across childhood [N2-F2][N4-R3]. Similarly, the evidence on gender moderation is thin: boys were more aggressive than girls in some samples, but gender did not consistently moderate SIP deficits in the provided material [N4-R3]. The practical implication is that SIP deficits should not be treated as a single “aggression” deficit, but as a staged system that can distinguish reactive from proactive aggression. In short, deficiencies in different stages of social information processing help distinguish reactive from proactive aggression by emphasizing different cognitive pathways: reactive aggression is best predicted by early-stage interpretation deficits, especially hostile attribution and poor cue use, while proactive aggression is better predicted by later-stage response generation and strategic processing deficits [N5-F3][N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-R5]. Deficits interact across stages through schemas, response access, and emotion regulation, and the model is best understood as a sequence in which each step can influence the next [N1-F1][N6-R5].
